qs.q: A 72-year-old patient presents with a 'magnetic' gait where the feet appear stuck to the floor, progressive dementia, and urinary incontinence. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step to confirm potential response to treatment?
o: Lumbar puncture removing 30 to 50 mL of CSF
Urgent burr hole drainage of subdural collections
Immediate placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt
qs.e: Improvement in symptoms after removing about 30 to 50 mL of CSF via lumbar puncture predicts a positive response to a shunt in normal pressure hydrocephalus. Direct shunting without this predictive tap is avoided until responsiveness is evaluated.
qs.s: Hydrocephalus: Causes, Presentation and CSF Diversion (Shunts): MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of painless lower abdominal swelling and dribbling incontinence. Clinical examination reveals a palpable, non-tender bladder extending to the umbilicus, and laboratory tests show a serum creatinine of 340 umol/L. What is the most critical management principle when relieving this patient's urinary retention?
o: Administer a stat dose of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors
Decompress the bladder slowly to avoid hypotension
Inflate a 30 mL balloon to tamponade potential bleeding
qs.e: In chronic retention, the bladder must be decompressed slowly to avoid complications like haemorrhage ex vacuo and hypotension. Rapid total drainage in chronic retention risks catastrophic haemodynamic shifts.
qs.s: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and Acute Urinary Retention: MCQs

qs.q: During a multidisciplinary clinic visit, a bowel management programme is established for a child with a myelomeningocele to handle fecal incontinence and constipation. Which combination of interventions forms the mainstay of this program?
qs.e: A bowel programme utilises enemas and laxatives to manage bowel function. Catheterisation is a urological intervention, not a bowel management strategy.
qs.s: Spina Bifida and Neural Tube Defects: Meningocele and Myelomeningocele: MCQs

qs.q: A 42-year-old woman with a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm presents with confusion, bilateral leg weakness, and urinary incontinence alongside abulia and personality changes. Which arterial territory is directly implicated in causing these specific localising signs?
qs.e: Anterior communicating artery aneurysms can affect the anterior cerebral artery territory, resulting in bilateral leg weakness, abulia, and personality changes due to involvement of the frontal lobes. Middle cerebral artery aneurysms typically cause contralateral face or hand weakness and aphasia.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A patient who suffered a severe subarachnoid hemorrhage following head trauma later develops progressive gait ataxia, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline. What is the most likely mechanism of this sequela?
o: Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid resorption in the subarachnoid space
Accumulation of tau-containing neurofibrillary tangles in frontal gyri
Recurrent bleeding from thin-walled subdural granulation vessels
Direct mechanical transection of the upper cervical spinal cord
qs.e: Posttraumatic hydrocephalus occurs due to the obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid resorption from subarachnoid hemorrhage. It presents with the classic triad of gait disturbance, incontinence, and cognitive changes, unlike spinal cord transection which causes motor level deficits.
qs.s: CNS Trauma Neuropathology: Fractures, Concussion & CTE: MCQs

qs.q: During the evaluation of a pediatric patient with urinary incontinence, a pediatric urologist distinguishes an orthotopic ureter from an ectopic ureter based on its insertion site. Where does an orthotopic ureter typically terminate?
qs.e: An orthotopic ureter terminates normally within the triangular trigone area of the bladder floor. Ectopic ureters insert outside this trigone, such as into the urethra or vagina.

qs.q: A 50-year-old man is evaluated for fecal incontinence following pelvic surgery. The physician tests the function of the sphincter that surrounds the lowest part of the anal canal. Which histological and functional feature describes this muscle?
qs.e: The external anal sphincter is composed of striated (skeletal) muscle under voluntary control, surrounding the lowest part of the anal canal. The internal anal sphincter is instead formed by smooth muscle.

ai.title: Urinary Incontinence in Adults
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Urinary incontinence is the involuntary loss of urine, ranging from occasional leaks to continuous dribbling. Accurate diagnosis requires history, bedside examination, and targeted investigations, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Incontinence is any involuntary urine loss that the patient cannot control. Diagnosis starts with a focused history and physical exam, confirming that the loss is urinary and not fecal or overflow from obstruction.
b: Ask about frequency, volume, triggers, and nocturnal episodes.
Use a voiding diary (3‑day) when possible.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire‑Short Form (ICIQ‑SF) or by pad count. Staging guides management intensity.
b: Mild: occasional leaks, <1 pad/day.
Moderate: daily leaks, 1‑2 pads/day.
Severe: continuous dribbling or >2 pads/day.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by mechanism: stress, urge, overflow, functional, and mixed. In low‑resource East African hospitals, common contributors include obstetric trauma, pelvic organ prolapse, untreated urinary tract infection, and neuro‑genic disease (e.g., HIV‑related neuropathy, spinal TB).
b: Stress: pelvic floor weakness after childbirth, prolapse.
Urge: overactive detrusor, untreated UTI, bladder stones.
Overflow: prostate enlargement, urethral stricture, neuro‑genic bladder.
Functional: mobility limitation, dementia, severe malaria.
Mixed: combination of stress and urge patterns.

sections.p: Patients report leakage with coughing, sneezing, or lifting (stress) or a sudden, strong urge with inability to reach the toilet (urge). Overflow presents as constant dribbling with a feeling of incomplete emptying.
b: Stress: leaks during increased intra‑abdominal pressure.
Urge: urgency with frequency, nocturia.

t.b: Detect infection, glucose, or hematuria; a positive nitrite or leukocyte esterase suggests UTI needing treatment.
Identifies prolapse, atrophic vaginitis, or prostate enlargement; guides anatomical cause.
Ensures safe use of anticholinergics; abnormal results may point to obstructive uropathy.
Shows bladder wall thickness, hydronephrosis, or stones; if unavailable, rely on clinical assessment and PVR.

sections.p: Uncontrolled incontinence can lead to skin breakdown, urinary tract infection, and social isolation. Urgent signs demand immediate attention.
b: Acute urinary retention.
Fever with flank pain (possible pyelonephritis).
New neurological deficits.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then use behavioural, mechanical, and pharmacological measures. Choose drugs that are safe in renal impairment and avoid those with anticholinergic burden in the elderly.
b: Lifestyle: fluid timing, bladder training, pelvic floor exercises.
Mechanical: pessary for prolapse (women), continence pads.
Pharmacology: antimuscarinics (oxybutynin) for urge; consider mirabegron if anticholinergic side‑effects likely.
Surgery: mid‑urethral sling for stress incontinence when conservative measures fail.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate symptoms after 4‑6 weeks of therapy. Prevent recurrence with continued pelvic floor training and early treatment of UTIs.
b: Document pad count and ICIQ‑SF score at each visit.
Educate on hygiene to avoid skin breakdown.

sections.p: Distinguish urinary incontinence from fecal incontinence, overflow due to constipation, and neuro‑genic bladder from spinal lesions.
b: Fecal incontinence: loss of stool, requires anorectal exam.
Overflow from constipation: hard stool impeding bladder emptying.

sections.p: A normal dipstick does not rule out a low‑grade infection; a low post‑void residual can be falsely reassuring in early obstruction.
b: UTI may be culture‑negative after recent antibiotics.
PVR measured by manual palpation is less accurate than bladder scan.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of bladder control after spinal injury

faq.q: Why is a pessary useful in stress incontinence?
faq.a: It supports the urethra and bladder neck, reducing leakage when surgery is not feasible.

faq.q: What is the first step when a patient presents with new‑onset urge incontinence?
faq.a: Rule out infection with a urine dipstick and treat any UTI before starting antimuscarinics.
Yes, diabetic neuropathy can produce a neuro‑genic bladder leading to overflow or urge symptoms.

exam: What bedside tests differentiate stress from urge incontinence? — Ask about triggers, perform cough stress test, and assess post‑void residual.
A 68‑year‑old woman with prolapse and daily leaks cannot afford surgery. What is the next best management? — Offer a vaginal pessary and pelvic floor exercises.
How does HIV‑related neuro‑genic bladder present and what investigation is essential? — Presents with urgency or overflow; measure post‑void residual to detect retention.
Why would you avoid oxybutynin in an elderly patient with narrow‑angle glaucoma? — Antimuscarinic effect can increase intra‑ocular pressure, worsening glaucoma.

Explain how normal‑pressure hydrocephalus can mimic urinary incontinence and how to distinguish it. — Triad includes gait disturbance and dementia; neuro‑imaging shows ventricular enlargement, unlike primary UI.
What lifestyle modification has the greatest impact on urge incontinence? — Timed voiding and bladder training to increase functional capacity.
When is surgical referral indicated for stress urinary incontinence? — After failure of conservative measures for ≥3 months and when the patient is fit for anesthesia.
